sheet-1.description: Sheet 1, drawn at 100 feet to an inch, covers the northern end of Hasbrouck Heights. The main area lies between Grandview Boulevard on the left and Burton Avenue, from beyond Stanley Avenue at the top down to Central Avenue at the bottom, crossed in turn by Stanley, Williams, Lawrence, Bell, Ottawa, Lasalle and Madison Avenues, with Collins Avenue running between Stanley and Williams. A narrow strip of blocks west of the Boulevard is drawn along the left edge. East of Burton Avenue the sheet continues from Ottawa Avenue down, across Terrace Avenue and Hasbrouck Avenue to Prospect Avenue. The northern blocks are laid out in long rows of narrow lots and are almost entirely vacant; scattered frame dwellings of two and two and a half storeys appear along Lawrence and Bell Avenues, and the blocks between Lasalle, Madison and Central Avenues are the most built up, with rows of frame houses, a few stuccoed, and one stone dwelling. Along Terrace Avenue stand the Hasbrouck Heights Garage, of concrete with an underground oil tank, and, at Central Avenue, the Old Homestead Hotel with a wagon shed. A steel tower with the fire alarm bell stands in block 152 near Stanley Avenue. Six-inch water pipes run in the cross streets and a twelve-inch main in Terrace Avenue. The upper right quarter of the sheet holds the title cartouche, a key map of the town with the borough lines of Lodi and Woodridge, notes on water facilities and the fire department, and the index of streets and specials; this panel is cut out of the mask. The legend key sits in block 83.
notes: Grandview Boulevard is now Boulevard.

The street lettered Hasbrouck Avenue on this sheet runs on the line of modern Prospect Street, and the street lettered Prospect Avenue on the line of modern Hasbrouck Avenue; the control points use the modern names by position.
Hasbrouck Heights Garage on Terrace Avenue; Old Homestead Hotel at Terrace and Central Avenues.
Steel tower with fire alarm bell in block 152.
Title dated October 1914; a receipt stamp in the upper right reads November 19, 1914.

Map, 100 ft to an inch. Stanley, Williams, Lawrence, Bell, Ottawa, Lasalle, Madison and Central Avs between Grandview Blvd (now Boulevard) and Burton Av; east of Burton from Ottawa down, Terrace, Hasbrouck and Prospect Avs. Upper right holds the title, key map of the town, water and fire notes and the street index (cut out of the mask). 1914 Hasbrouck Av is the line of modern Prospect Street and 1914 Prospect Av is modern Hasbrouck Avenue (names swapped against OpenStreetMap). One part.

sheet-2-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 2, drawn at 100 feet to an inch, covers the west-central part of Hasbrouck Heights from Central Avenue at the top to Raymond Avenue at the bottom, between the west edge of the sheet and a row of blocks east of Grandview Boulevard. Oak Grove Avenue runs down the sheet, and the cross streets are Central, Washington, Kipp, Jefferson, Franklin, Hamilton, Walter and Division Avenues. West of Oak Grove Avenue the blocks (9 to 14 and 73) are laid out in narrow lots and are mostly vacant, with a few frame dwellings and flats along Washington, Kipp and Jefferson Avenues; Franklin Avenue is marked not opened west of Oak Grove. Between Oak Grove Avenue and the Boulevard the blocks are well built up with two- and two-and-a-half-storey frame dwellings. The Boulevard frontage is the town's business street: stores at its corners include groceries, meat markets, a bakery, a barber, a drug store and post office, billiards, shoe and tailor shops, a plumber, a liquor store, an undertaker, a wagon shed and a motion picture theatre between Franklin and Hamilton Avenues. East of the Boulevard stand a Roman Catholic church in block 46, the Pioneer Club in block 45, a five-and-ten-cent store and a bakery, and the Hasbrouck Heights Field Club house in block 40. A steel tower for the fire alarm bell stands near Oak Grove and Kipp Avenues. Six-inch water pipes run in the streets. The lower left of the sheet is a separately drawn inset (part 2), cut off by a heavy line.
notes: Washington Avenue is now Washington Place; Raymond Avenue is now Raymond Street; Grandview Boulevard is now Boulevard.
Franklin Avenue west of Oak Grove Avenue is marked not opened.
Roman Catholic church (block 46), Pioneer Club (block 45), H. H. Field Club club house (block 40), motion picture theatre on the Boulevard.
The junction of Division and Oak Grove Avenues was not used as control: the detector placed it about 11 m from the fit.

Map, 100 ft to an inch. Part 1: Central to Raymond Avs (Washington Av now Washington Place, Raymond Av now Raymond Street) between the west edge and Grandview Blvd, crossed by Oak Grove Av. Part 2 (lower left inset, behind a heavy line): Williams, Lawrence and Bell Avs between Burton Av and Hasbrouck Av (modern Prospect Street), with Terrace Av.

sheet-2-2.description: Part 2 of sheet 2 is an inset in the lower left corner of the sheet, separated from the main map by a heavy line and drawn at 100 feet to an inch. It shows the northern end of town east of Burton Avenue: Williams Avenue along the top, Lawrence Avenue and Bell Avenue across the middle and bottom, with Burton Avenue at the left edge, Terrace Avenue and, further east, Hasbrouck Avenue, which is marked not opened. The blocks are large and only partly built: block 92 between Williams and Lawrence Avenues and block 91 between Lawrence and Bell Avenues carry a handful of two- and two-and-a-half-storey frame dwellings, one with a small brick outbuilding, and garages; block 90 south of Bell Avenue is cut by the bottom of the sheet. East of Terrace Avenue, block 125 is a long open tract with two dwellings and its own north arrow, and block 126 between Hasbrouck Avenue and the heavy border has two dwellings near Williams Avenue. A twelve-inch water main runs in Terrace Avenue and six-inch pipes in Lawrence and Bell Avenues. The area continues the east side of sheet 1, whose Burton Avenue frontage it adjoins.
notes: The street lettered Hasbrouck Avenue here runs on the line of modern Prospect Street (the control point at Williams Avenue uses the modern name).
Hasbrouck Avenue is marked not opened.

Map, 100 ft to an inch. Part 1: Central to Raymond Avs (Washington Av now Washington Place, Raymond Av now Raymond Street) between the west edge and Grandview Blvd, crossed by Oak Grove Av. Part 2 (lower left inset, behind a heavy line): Williams, Lawrence and Bell Avs between Burton Av and Hasbrouck Av (modern Prospect Street), with Terrace Av.

sheet-3.description: Sheet 3, drawn at 100 feet to an inch, covers the centre of Hasbrouck Heights from Central Avenue at the top to Raymond Avenue at the bottom. Its left edge is the east side of Grandview Boulevard; Burton Avenue runs down the middle of the western half and Terrace Avenue down the centre, bending south-east below Walter Avenue. The cross streets are Central, Washington, Kipp, Jefferson, Franklin, Hamilton, Walter and Division Avenues. West of Terrace Avenue the blocks are closely built with two- and two-and-a-half-storey frame dwellings, a few of brick or concrete block, and the town's institutions: the First Reformed Church at Washington Avenue and the Boulevard, the Episcopal church near Jefferson and Burton Avenues, the brick Franklin School with its auditorium in block 43, the Municipal Building with the fire department and hose tower on Hamilton Avenue, the Baptist church at Hamilton and Burton Avenues, the M.E. church and the Borough League Library on Division Avenue, dog kennels and the People's Tennis Court near Raymond Avenue. East of Terrace Avenue, at the top, Michigan Avenue and Washington Place cross Hasbrouck, Prospect and Cedar Avenues in mostly vacant lots; Ravine Avenue curves from Washington Place to 3rd Street, with the Hasbrouck Inn hotel and stores near Terrace Avenue, the printing office of the Hasbrouck Heights News Letter, and L. Holmsted's Sons' machine shop in block 108. Below Franklin Avenue large blocks 103 and 104 are divided by Berkshire Road and hold a few dwellings; the lower right corner is a peach orchard with a fruit packing building. Six-inch water pipes run in the cross streets and a twelve-inch main in Terrace Avenue.
notes: Washington Avenue is now Washington Place; Raymond Avenue is now Raymond Street.

Prospect Avenue east of Terrace runs on the line of modern Hasbrouck Avenue, and Cedar Avenue on the line of modern Garrison Avenue; Hasbrouck Avenue between Michigan Avenue and Washington Place has no modern counterpart in the reference data.
Kipp Avenue now continues east of Terrace Avenue through block 108; in 1914 it ended at Terrace.

First Reformed Church, Episcopal church, Baptist church, M.E. church, Franklin School, Municipal Building with fire department, Borough League Library, Hasbrouck Inn, Hasbrouck Heights News Letter printing office, L. Holmsted's Sons machine shop.

Map, 100 ft to an inch. Central to Raymond Avs between Grandview Blvd (left edge) and Terrace Av, with Burton Av; east of Terrace: Michigan Av, Washington Pl, Ravine Av, Berkshire Road, and Hasbrouck, Prospect (modern Hasbrouck Avenue) and Cedar (modern Garrison Avenue) Avs at the top; 3rd St at the right edge. One part.

sheet-4-1.description: Part 1 of sheet 4, drawn at 100 feet to an inch, covers the southern end of Hasbrouck Heights from Raymond Avenue at the top to Lincoln Avenue and the borough line with Woodridge at the bottom. Grandview Boulevard crosses the left side diagonally; Burton Avenue runs down from Raymond to Passaic Avenue and Summit Street from Springfield to Lincoln Avenue; Terrace Avenue runs down the right-hand side, leaving its old line at Passaic Avenue on a diagonal past Euclid Square and Main Street. The cross streets are Raymond Avenue, Henry Street, Passaic, Springfield, Columbus, Cleveland, Harrison, Roosevelt and Lincoln Avenues. The blocks are laid out in long rows of narrow lots and are thinly built, with scattered two- and two-and-a-half-storey frame dwellings, several stuccoed, a private garage and stable with a billiard room on Henry Street, a concrete-block dwelling with store on Passaic Avenue, chicken houses in block 51 and a few brick and stone buildings near Euclid Square. A steel tower for the fire alarm bell stands in block 33. West of the Boulevard, Harrison Avenue is marked not opened, and blocks 16 to 19 and 74 are only partly drawn, with a note of two-storey frame dwellings beyond. A twelve-inch water main runs in Terrace Avenue and six-inch pipes in the cross streets. The boundary line between Hasbrouck Heights and Woodridge runs along the bottom of the sheet, south of Lincoln Avenue. The upper right corner holds a separate inset (part 2).
notes: Raymond Avenue is now Raymond Street; Grandview Boulevard is now Boulevard.
The old line of Terrace Avenue between Henry Street and Passaic Avenue survives as Old Terrace Avenue; the 1914 diagonal is the present Terrace Avenue.
Harrison Avenue west of the Boulevard and Passaic Avenue east of Terrace Avenue are marked not opened.
Woodridge is now the Borough of Wood-Ridge.
The junction of Cleveland and Terrace Avenues at Euclid Square was not used as control (detected about 14 m from the fit).

Map, 100 ft to an inch. Part 1: Raymond to Lincoln Avs between Grandview Blvd and Terrace Av, with Burton Av, Henry St, Summit St, Euclid Square and Main St; borough line with Woodridge (now Wood-Ridge) along the bottom. Part 2 (upper right inset): Hasbrouck Heights Embroidery Works on the east side of Terrace Av at the Woodridge line, with no street junction.

sheet-4-2.description: Part 2 of sheet 4 is an inset in the upper right corner of the sheet, inside a heavy border, drawn at 100 feet to an inch with its own north arrow. It shows a short stretch of Terrace Avenue, carrying a twelve-inch water main, where it crosses the boundary line between Hasbrouck Heights and Woodridge, with the end of Lincoln Avenue lettered beside it. East of Terrace Avenue, just north of the borough line, stand the buildings of the Hasbrouck Heights Embroidery Works: a group of frame buildings of one to two and a half storeys and one brick building, with fire pails, electric power and gas and electric lighting noted. The surrounding ground is marked no exposures on every side. The inset lies just beyond the right edge of the main map, east of Terrace Avenue at the south end of town, and the main sheet's title cartouche overlaps its upper part.
notes: Hasbrouck Heights Embroidery Works.
Placed from one point carried from part 1 (Terrace Avenue at the borough line) and the scale and rotation of part 1; low confidence.
Woodridge is now the Borough of Wood-Ridge.
